newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: TOP SAFRICA POLICE ORDERED MURDER COVER UP-WITNESS.
newsitem.headline: TOP SAFRICA POLICE ORDERED MURDER COVER UP-WITNESS.

text.p: Senior South African police officers ordered and assisted a self-confessed killer to cover up police attrocities, a key witness in the murder trial of an apartheid-era assassin said on Monday.

Lawyers for the former commander of the covert Vlakplaas police unit near Pretoria, Dirk Coetzee, had subpoenaed the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for the testimony by Joe Mamasela, who had worked as an informer at the unit.

The commission, set up to try to heal South Africa's divided past by investigating human rights abuses committed by all sides during 30 years of white minority rule, initially refused to hand over Mamasela's testimony, as it was given behind closed doors.

But Judge Piet Combrinck earlier on Monday ordered the commission to release the testimony, saying Coetzee was entitled to the information under constitutional guarantees of the right to a free and fair trial.

Mamasela, who took part in the murder and has turned state witness in exchange for indemnity, told the court grisly details of the stabbing and beating to death of Mxenge and how senior officers later ordered a cover up.
After one of the accused Almond Nofomela spilt the beans shortly before he was due to be executed in 1989 for an unrelated murder, crisis meetings were called by senior officers, Mamasela said.
"It was devastating. In Pretoria headquarters it was chaos, there was a beehive of movement from the junior officers right up to the generals.

"At the meetings we were told to cover up and what to say to the commission (probing the hitsquad allegations). It was decided we must all stand together and not one of us should support (Nofomela)," Mamasela said.
Meetings for all those involved in the Mxenge murder were chaired by Brigadiers Krappies Engelbrecht and Nick van Rensburg, he said.
Mamasela said all he had to do was sign affidavits prepared on his behalf by the brigadiers which denied any involvement in the murder.
"I was presented with documents that I just had to sign... the denials were already filled in," he said.
The commission, which finishes its work at the end of this year, is able to grant amnesty to perpetrators who come forward and give full and honest accounts of their deeds.

Coetzee and two of his four co-accused, Nofomela and David Tshikalanga, applied to the commission last year for amnesty for the brutal murder of Mxenge, whose family has waged a vociferous campaign against amnesty for his killers.
A decision on their amnesty request is expected in June.
